content.text: {"grade": 6, "complete": true, "main_gap": "Q is defined as the primes dividing A, but the lemma and its proof only work (and are clearly intended) with Q = all primes at most A; with the literal definition the lemma is false.", "errors": [{"description": "Definition of Q is misstated. Written as primes dividing A, but the lemma proof repeatedly uses 'all prime factors of x at most A ⇒ σ(x)=P(x)' and 'every prime in σ(b) is at most A / every prime in P(x)\\σ(x) exceeds A', which need Q = {primes ≤ A}. With the literal Q the lemma fails (A=15: σ(18)={3} is not good, as 20 is a term). The author's own 'hypotheses' section confirms the intended Q; fix is one line.", "quote": "Q=\\{p:p\\text{ is prime and }p\\mid A\\}"}, {"description": "Unused false remark, contradicted by the author's own counterexample (A=15, terms 18 vs skipped 21). Not load-bearing but adds to the definitional confusion.", "quote": "Only the primes dividing \\(A\\) can matter here, because every term shares a prime factor with \\(A=a_1\\)."}], "notes": "With Q read as primes ≤ A, every step checks: (1) characterizes terms ≥A by goodness of support; the erasure lemma (via m=Rp^k<x and induction on terms) is correct; L=∏Q gives exact periodicity from A onward, yielding a_{n+T}=a_n+L for all n. Deducted one point for the inconsistent definition."}
